chapter: A Different Way — A Brief Theology of Technology
idea: Technology is a God-given expression of human image-bearing — created good, distorted by sin, and redirected through builders formed by redemption.
application: When work feels spiritually meaningless, re-frame tasks by their formative purpose: what this work trains in the builder, not just what it ships.

chapter: A Different Way — Four Gospel Lenses
idea: Read technology through the four-part Gospel lens: creation (a calling to make), deception (how making distorts), redemption (how builders get reclaimed), restoration (where making finally goes).
application: Use the lens as a quick review grid: does this plan create faithfully, hide a distortion, or need redemption in how it gets built?

chapter: The Way of Technology — Everyone Is a Builder Now
idea: Everyone is a builder now: technology is the skilled practice of creating that shapes both world and the maker.
application: Treat tool-building tasks with intent — every small script or app the user creates is practice of a craft that forms them.

chapter: Three Ancient Enemies — The Magic Machine Myth
idea: The Magic Machine Myth: believing advanced technology is scarce, indispensable, and god-like — products become surrogate gods people trust too much.
application: When designs make people dependent on opaque automation, propose honesty surfaces (explain what it does, where it fails).

chapter: Three Ancient Enemies — The Limitless Self
idea: The Limitless Self: our tools promise infinite capability — rushing past the limits of time, body, and needing others.
application: In scheduling and studies, respect human limits: sleep, sabbath, and bodies are design constraints — not bottlenecks to hack around.

chapter: Three Ancient Enemies — The Killer App Trap
idea: The Killer App Trap: the belief that technology itself will save, fix, or become the ultimate answer for human problems.
application: Before pitching a project as transformative, ask what human community it actually serves — the app is a tool, not a savior.

chapter: A Way of Being Redemptive — Reckless Technology
idea: Reckless technology ('move fast, break things') optimizes for spectacle and speed while who gets hurt becomes an afterthought.
application: When urgency pressure mounts, check what the speed costs other people — running over teammates isn't a plan, it's damage.

chapter: A Way of Being Redemptive — Responsible Technology
idea: Responsible technology ('slow down, fix things') reduces harm, shares power, and promotes human flourishing — but stops at fix-mode.
application: As a baseline standard for suggested work: accessibility, privacy, and fair handling are failure conditions, never nice-to-haves.

idea: Redemptive builders surrender power: they release claims to control, invite accountability, and give people agency over technologies shaping them.
application: In product decisions, prefer more user control (export, settings, transparency) over more silent influence over users.

idea: People are image-bearers, not users or data: refuse to reduce them to metrics or means; every person affected belongs to God before the product.
application: Treat metrics-driven suggestions cautiously — if an idea treats humans as levers, flag it before it becomes practice.

idea: Direct technology work toward God's mission — serving neighbors and strengthening faithful community, not just announcing greatness.
application: Purpose-check big decisions: whose problem does this solve, and on what horizon? Prefer plainly-helpful over applause-generating.

idea: Lament: patiently refuse to rush past pain — walk into what's broken before proposing what to ship.
application: Before designing a solution, schedule reflection time; enter the user's actual pain to expose false assumptions in the plan.

idea: Discern: seek wisdom before choosing a response — not every good idea is your task to build.
application: Run captures and ideas through a discernment step: does it align with the user's calling, capacity, and season before it enters the matrix.

idea: Build faithfully in dependence on the Spirit: make with skill, honesty, and openness about what you can't control.
application: Ship with integrity: small honest increments beat big boasts; document limitations as clearly as features.

idea: Steward what you release: take responsibility for what your work continues to do in the world after it ships.
application: Attach maintenance and monitoring follow-ups to shipped work — responsibility continues beyond done.

idea: The final measure of technology work is who the builder becomes — the practice of creating is formation, not just production.
application: In weekly reviews, evaluate formation alongside output: patience, honesty, and love growing? That is the real success metric.
